events.description: The Donghak Peasant Revolution of 1894 was the largest uprising in Joseon history: tens of thousands of peasants under the preacher Jeon Bong-jun swept through Jeolla Province, defeating the provincial army and demanding an end to corruption, taxation, slavery, and foreign influence. The Joseon court's panicked call for Qing troops to suppress it triggered the Sino-Japanese War.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: In the territories they controlled, the Donghak rebels did not just loot — they set up administrative councils called "jipgang-so" that distributed food, adjudicated disputes, and ran local governance. Jeon Bong-jun was captured, tried, and executed in 1895; he is now considered a major figure of Korean nationalist history. The rebels' original target was a single corrupt magistrate named Jo Byeong-gap, whose extortion of local farmers sparked the January 1894 revolt that grew into a national revolution within months.

events.label: First Sino-Japanese War
events.description: The First Sino-Japanese War (August 1894 – April 1895) was a comprehensive Japanese military victory, fought primarily on Korean and Manchurian soil, that ended five centuries of Chinese suzerainty over Korea and announced Japan as East Asia's dominant power. China paid a massive indemnity and ceded Taiwan.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The war lasted only about seven months and shocked the world — China had been universally assumed to be the stronger power. Japan sank the Chinese fleet at the Battle of the Yellow Sea in September 1894 and then invaded Manchuria itself. The Treaty of Shimonoseki forced China to formally recognize Korea as "independent" (meaning available for Japanese absorption), pay 200 million taels of silver in indemnity, and cede Taiwan, the Pescadores Islands, and the Liaodong Peninsula (though Russia, Germany, and France immediately forced Japan to return the Liaodong Peninsula in the "Triple Intervention").

events.label: Gabo Reforms
events.description: The Gabo Reforms of 1894–96 were the most sweeping legal changes in Joseon history: the slave system was abolished, the gwageo (civil service exam) was abolished, the four-class yangban-commoner hierarchy was dissolved, and a modern Western-style cabinet replaced the old bureaucracy — all imposed under Japanese pressure after the Sino-Japanese War.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Historians still debate how much of the Gabo program was genuinely wanted by Korean reformers versus simply imposed by Japan as a pretext for transforming Korean institutions to suit Japanese interests. The abolition of slavery in particular came centuries later than in many other societies — the Joseon slave system had held roughly a third of the population at its peak (Chapter 2). The reforms formally abolished Confucian remarriage restrictions on women, a change so radical it scandalized much of the Korean elite even as they accepted other modernizing measures.

events.label: Assassination of Queen Min
events.description: Before dawn on October 8, 1895, roughly fifty Japanese assassins — army personnel, right-wing civilian thugs, and Korean collaborators — organized by Japanese Minister Miura Goro broke into Gyeongbokgung Palace, found Queen Min in her chambers, killed her with swords, dragged her body into the palace garden, and burned it.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Miura Goro was recalled to Japan, tried, and acquitted on a technicality — Japan essentially suffered no consequences for murdering a sitting queen inside her own palace. Queen Min (posthumously Empress Myeongseong) had pivoted away from Japan toward Russia after the Sino-Japanese War, which is why Miura considered her an obstacle worth killing. King Gojong, terrified, fled to the Russian legation the following February and governed from a foreign embassy for over a year — an almost unimaginably degrading spectacle for a sitting monarch.

events.label: Korean Empire Proclaimed
events.description: In October 1897, after returning from over a year of shelter in the Russian legation, King Gojong proclaimed himself Emperor of the Daehan Jeguk ("Korean Empire"), asserting sovereignty equal to Japan and China and formally terminating any subordinate relationship to Qing China.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The new imperial title was symbolically important: by calling himself emperor (not king), Gojong claimed the same rank as the Chinese and Japanese rulers and rejected the Confucian tributary hierarchy that had made Korea formally subordinate to China. The Korean Empire lasted only thirteen years and was never genuinely independent. Gojong's strategy of playing Japan, Russia, and the US against each other failed when all three powers ultimately chose their own interests over Korean sovereignty.

events.label: Russo-Japanese War
events.description: The Russo-Japanese War (1904–05) was the first modern war in which an Asian power defeated a major European empire — Japan crushed Russia on land in Manchuria and destroyed the Russian Baltic Fleet at the Battle of Tsushima (May 1905) after it had sailed halfway around the world. The Treaty of Portsmouth, mediated by US President Theodore Roosevelt, gave Japan a free hand in Korea.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The Battle of Tsushima was one of the most decisive naval battles in modern history: Japan destroyed virtually the entire Russian Baltic Fleet — 21 of 35 warships sunk, 7 captured — in under two days, losing only three torpedo boats. Roosevelt won the Nobel Peace Prize for brokering the Treaty of Portsmouth, even though the peace effectively handed Korea to Japan. In a separate secret agreement (the Taft-Katsura Memorandum), the US acknowledged Japanese dominance in Korea in exchange for Japanese recognition of American control of the Philippines — Korea traded for the Philippines.

events.label: Eulsa Treaty
events.description: The Eulsa Treaty of November 17, 1905 stripped Korea of its right to conduct its own foreign policy and installed a Japanese Resident-General with supervisory authority over the Korean government. Five Korean ministers — the "Five Eulsa Traitors" — signed under direct Japanese military pressure while Emperor Gojong refused personally but could not stop them.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The newspaper editor Jang Ji-yeon published a famous editorial titled "Today We Cry" the day the treaty was announced, which became one of the iconic texts of Korean resistance. Senior official Min Yeong-hwan went home after the signing, wrote a suicide note calling for continued resistance, and slit his throat — one of several prominent suicides in protest. Korea's diplomatic offices abroad (in the US, France, and elsewhere) were closed down within months, leaving Korea with no voice in the international community.

events.label: Hague Secret Mission
events.description: In 1907 Emperor Gojong secretly dispatched three envoys to the Second Hague Peace Conference to denounce the Eulsa Treaty before the world's powers — but Japan pressured the conference organizers to refuse them an official hearing. One envoy died in the Hague; Japan used the episode as a pretext to force Gojong to abdicate.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The three envoys were Yi Sang-seol (a former prime minister), Yi Jun (a lawyer and activist), and Yi Wi-jong (a diplomat). Yi Jun's death at the Hague has never been definitively explained — the Korean nationalist account says he committed suicide in despair after being refused; some accounts claim it was illness. Gojong was forced to abdicate in favor of his mentally limited son Sunjong, who became the last Joseon king and never held real power. The Hague mission's failure ended the last realistic hope of international intervention on Korea's behalf.

events.label: An Jung-geun's Assassination of Ito
events.description: On October 26, 1909, Korean independence fighter An Jung-geun shot former Japanese Resident-General Ito Hirobumi three times at close range on the platform of Harbin railway station in Manchuria. Ito died within minutes. An was tried, unrepentant, and hanged by Japanese authorities in March 1910.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: While awaiting execution, An Jung-geun wrote an unfinished political treatise titled "On East Asian Peace" arguing for a Korea-China-Japan confederation of equals against Western imperialism — a remarkable piece of political thinking from a condemned man. He was also a fine calligrapher, and several pieces of his prison-cell calligraphy survive as objects of veneration in Korea. An memorial was built at Harbin railway station in 2014 with Chinese government cooperation — a politically pointed act given ongoing Japan-China tensions — and Japan officially objected to its construction.

events.label: Japanese Annexation of Korea
events.description: On August 22, 1910, Japan formally annexed Korea under the Japan-Korea Treaty of 1910, ending the Joseon dynasty and the Korean Empire after 518 years of rule. The last emperor Sunjong was placed under house arrest; Korean prime minister Yi Wan-yong signed the document for Korea.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Yi Wan-yong, who signed the annexation treaty, became the most reviled figure in modern Korean history — "Wangyong" became a common insult meaning traitor. Korean sovereignty would not be restored for 35 years, until Japan's defeat in World War II in August 1945. The 518-year run of the Joseon dynasty outlasted the Roman Empire (roughly 500 years from Augustus to the fall of the West), the Ming dynasty (276 years), and the Romanov dynasty (304 years) — one of the longest uninterrupted political regimes in premodern world history.

events.label: Kim Jeong-ho's Daedongyeojido
events.description: Cartographer Kim Jeong-ho, a commoner who walked the country mapping it himself, produced the Daedongyeojido in 1861 — a 22-volume folding atlas that, when assembled, formed an 11-foot map of the Korean peninsula astonishingly accurate by modern standards.

events.label: Pansori Folk Opera
events.description: Pansori, an unaccompanied solo singing-and-storytelling tradition performed by a single vocalist with a single drummer, emerged among commoner audiences in the southwest. The five surviving pansori epics, now UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage, are the great vernacular literature of Joseon.

events.label: Hong Dae-yong's Cosmology
events.description: Hong Dae-yong (1731–1783) met Jesuit astronomers in Beijing in 1765, then returned to Korea and wrote the Damheonseo — arguing that the earth rotates once every twenty-four hours and speculating that intelligent beings probably exist on other worlds, positions he reasoned out himself from first principles.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Western astronomy had not yet made Copernican rotation an orthodoxy at the time Hong made his arguments — he was working ahead of the consensus, not borrowing it. His extraterrestrial speculation came from an analogy: if Earth is a sphere spinning in space, the universe is probably similar throughout, so why would Earth alone produce intelligent life? This is a remarkably modern line of reasoning for an eighteenth-century Korean scholar who had access to only the books available at the Qing court.

events.label: Nobi Slave System
events.description: The nobi were Joseon's hereditary slaves — roughly a third of the early-dynasty population — divided between gwannobi (state-owned, serving palaces and offices) and sanobi (privately owned by yangban households). Nobi status was inherited from either parent and could only be escaped through extraordinary royal favor, military service, or the legal reforms of the late dynasty.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Major yangban households might own hundreds or even thousands of sanobi organized into agricultural communities working family estates — a slave proportion comparable to or higher than classical Rome or the antebellum American South. Nobi had limited legal personhood: they could marry other nobi and own modest property, but they could be bought, sold, and willed to heirs. The government nobi were emancipated in 1801 when the new regime burned the slave registers — about 36,000 people freed in a single unilateral act — but private nobi slavery wasn't formally abolished until the Gabo Reforms of 1894.

events.label: Women in Confucian Joseon
events.description: Joseon's adoption of Neo-Confucian family law over the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries rolled back rights Korean women had held under Goryeo — equal inheritance, bilateral kinship, easy remarriage — replacing them with strict patrilineal succession, mandatory household seclusion for yangban women, and near-erasure from official genealogies.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Under Goryeo, brides lived in the wife's family home until the first child was born; Joseon reversed this, moving brides permanently into the husband's household as teenagers. A remarried widow's children were legally barred from taking the gwageo exam — an effective life sentence of poverty for any yangban widow who hoped her descendants might hold office. Korean historian Martina Deuchler documented how this transformation was so thorough that by the late seventeenth century Joseon had become more strictly patrilineal than China itself, the source of the ideology.
